text.title: EARS Adoption Failure Modes
text.summary: Seven ways an EARS rollout fails, each with the observable symptom, the cause, and the rule that prevents it. Five of the seven are adoption failures, not grammar failures.

failure.symptom: Requirements pass the linter, ship, and the feature is still wrong. Confidence in the spec rises while defect rate does not fall.
failure.cause: The grammar was sold, internally or externally, as a correctness check. "When a customer submits the checkout form, the payment service shall charge the customer twice." parses, classifies event-driven and trips zero rules.
failure.prevention: Say the limit out loud in the tooling, not in a footnote. Warnings-only by default, `verification_method` still mandatory, review still mandatory. A linter that is believed to be more than it is does more damage than no linter.

failure.symptom: The check is disabled in week one and never re-enabled. Someone adds `# noqa`-equivalent suppressions everywhere, or removes the hook entirely.
failure.cause: The rule set was made blocking before its false-positive rate was measured on a real corpus. W105 (pronouns), W106/W107 (`if` vs `when`) and W112 (weasel verbs) are vocabulary heuristics with no corpus behind them.
failure.prevention: Default warnings-only, exit 0. `--strict` is opt-in and CI-only. No blocking pre-commit hook in v1. Run the rule set across every existing `spec.md` and tune before `--strict` is offered to anyone. A linter's credibility is spent entirely on its first false positive.

failure.symptom: Non-technical stakeholders stop writing requirements at all. Requirements arrive as Slack messages again.
failure.cause: A founder typed "must" or "will" and the tool rejected the sentence. The perceived message is "you are writing this wrong", which is what kills adoption of every requirements discipline ever shipped.
failure.prevention: Keep `shall` as the stored canonical form and never require a human to type it. Normalise `must`/`will`/`has to`/`needs to` → `shall` at info level, auto-fixable. Accept comma-less ALL-CAPS input leniently, never canonicalise it. Better still: ask three plain questions (what must be true first / what sets this off / what does the app do), generate the sentence, and have the author confirm it. Reading `shall` is not a barrier; writing it is.

failure.symptom: Negative-path acceptance criteria are written with `When` and happy paths with `If`. Test suites end up with error cases in the happy-path file.
failure.cause: Both forms parse, so nothing catches it. The vocabulary heuristics catch the obvious half ("When the payment fails") and miss the rest.
failure.prevention: Generate the keyword from `user-flows.md` instead of detecting it. The happy-path / negative-path split in that file already encodes the distinction exactly; throwing that information away and then trying to recover it with a regex is the actual bug.

failure.symptom: A test fails and nobody can say which requirement failed. Coverage audits show one id mapped to two unrelated test files.
failure.cause: A compound response (`shall display X and retain Y`) or a second `shall` bundled two obligations under one identifier, usually because splitting felt like padding.
failure.prevention: One `shall` per statement, compound responses split. This is the cheapest and highest-yield rule in the set, and it is the failure non-technical authors actually make — the barrier was never vocabulary, it is decomposition.

failure.symptom: The spec fills with sentences like "The system shall be modular" and "The product shall be intuitive for non-technical users". Reviewers stop reading the requirement section.
failure.cause: A maximalist rollout forced goals, invariants and quality adjectives through the grammar because the grammar was mandatory. They pass and mean nothing.
failure.prevention: Refuse and route: goals to `roadmap.md` with a measured target, invariants to `project-spec/`, unmeasurable adjectives rewritten or dropped. Where an NFR genuinely is not a system response to a condition, record `ears_pattern: n-a` with a reason — visible, countable, arguable.

failure.symptom: Production hits a state nobody wrote a requirement for. Every individual requirement was valid EARS.
failure.cause: An `If X` requirement exists with no requirement covering `not X`. Terzakis's canonical case: "If a boot disk is detected in the system, the software shall boot from it." — and if it is not present?
failure.prevention: Accept that this is invisible to a line-level linter and schedule the set-level coverage pass as a separate check over the whole file. Do not let a clean line-level report be read as a complete requirement set.
